clinicalPearls: Maternally inherited mitochondrial disorder, most often from one of three primary mtDNA point mutations affecting complex I (m.11778, m.3460, m.14484)
Typically affects young adult males with subacute, painless, severe central visual loss in one eye followed by the fellow eye within weeks to months
Acute phase shows peripapillary telangiectatic microangiopathy, disc hyperaemia, and swelling of the retinal nerve fibre layer without leakage on angiography
Progresses to optic atrophy with a dense central or centrocaecal scotoma and impaired colour vision
Incomplete penetrance and marked male predominance indicate modifying genetic and environmental factors
Smoking and heavy alcohol use are recognised triggers/aggravators and should be avoided
The m.14484 mutation carries the best chance of spontaneous visual recovery
reference.pathophysiology: Leber hereditary optic neuropathy is caused by pathogenic point mutations in mitochondrial DNA that impair complex I of the respiratory chain, reducing ATP production and increasing oxidative stress. Retinal ganglion cells, particularly the small fibres of the papillomacular bundle, are exquisitely dependent on mitochondrial energy and are preferentially vulnerable. Energy failure and oxidative damage trigger dysfunction and then apoptotic loss of these ganglion cells, producing the characteristic central visual loss and subsequent optic atrophy. Incomplete penetrance and the male bias reflect the influence of mitochondrial heteroplasmy, nuclear modifiers, hormonal factors, and environmental triggers.
additionalDifferentials: Bilateral sequential optic neuropathy from other causes
additionalInvestigations: Mitochondrial DNA testing for the primary LHON point mutations
Optical coherence tomography of the retinal nerve fibre layer and ganglion cell complex
Automated perimetry documenting central or centrocaecal scotomata
Fundus fluorescein angiography (characteristically no leakage despite disc appearance)
MRI of brain and orbits to exclude compressive or demyelinating causes
redFlags: Rapid sequential involvement of the second eye
Atypical features (pain, response to steroids, or optic disc leakage) suggesting an alternative diagnosis
Systemic or neurological signs indicating a 'LHON-plus' phenotype
Continued smoking or alcohol exposure accelerating visual loss
reference.prognosis: Most patients suffer severe and permanent bilateral central visual loss, although a minority recover useful vision, most commonly those with the m.14484 mutation and younger patients; avoidance of smoking and excess alcohol and emerging gene and pharmacological therapies may modify outcomes.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing it as atypical optic neuritis and giving prolonged unhelpful immunosuppression
Failing to counsel on maternal inheritance and the risk to relatives
Overlooking modifiable triggers such as smoking and alcohol in carriers
Not recognising the disc appearance can mimic true papilloedema early on
management: Consider idebenone, a synthetic short-chain quinone, particularly during the acute or subacute phase to support residual vision
Strongly advise smoking cessation and avoidance of heavy alcohol, which are recognised triggers and aggravators
Provide low-vision aids and visual rehabilitation for the central scotoma and impaired colour vision
Monitor both eyes with optical coherence tomography and perimetry, anticipating sequential involvement of the fellow eye
Offer genetic counselling explaining maternal mitochondrial inheritance, incomplete penetrance and male predominance, with assessment of at-risk maternal relatives
Refer to neuro-ophthalmology and clinical genetics, and consider emerging mitochondrial-targeted gene therapies within specialist or trial settings
